defs: A decoy system designed to attract, detect, or study attackers.

course.learn: Deception technologies create fake resources that attract or reveal attackers. Because legitimate users should not normally interact with them, activity involving the decoy is highly suspicious.
course.why: Decoys can provide early detection, waste attacker time, and reveal tactics without exposing real assets.
course.example: A fake database credential is placed where only an intruder scanning sensitive files would find it; using it generates an alert.
course.exam: Honeypot = decoy system; honeynet = decoy network; honeyfile = decoy file; honeytoken = decoy data/credential.

breakdown.explanation: A honeypot is a decoy system deliberately made attractive to attackers so defenders can detect, distract, or study them.
A honeynet is a network of multiple deception systems that gives defenders a broader view of attacker movement and techniques.
A honeyfile is a decoy document or data file intended to reveal unauthorized browsing, copying, or exfiltration.
A honeytoken is fake data—often a credential, API key, database value, or identifier—that has no legitimate use. Any use of it is suspicious.

course.learn: A honeynet is a network of multiple deception systems that gives defenders a broader view of attacker movement and techniques.
course.why: It can reveal multi-stage behavior that a single honeypot cannot show.
course.example: An attacker compromises a fake workstation and then attempts lateral movement into a decoy database server inside the same honeynet.
course.exam: Honeynet = multiple interconnected decoys, not merely one fake server.

course.learn: A honeyfile is a decoy document or data file intended to reveal unauthorized browsing, copying, or exfiltration.
course.why: Legitimate workflows should not need the file, so opening or moving it can trigger investigation.
course.example: A file named “Executive_Salaries.xlsx” contains fake records and alerts security when accessed from an unusual account.
course.exam: File/document decoy = honeyfile; credential/string decoy = honeytoken.

breakdown.explanation: The goal is to discover and clearly document the condition so the organization can decide what action to take next.

slides.title: Honeytoken
points: Track lateral movement within your network
slides.raw:
Honeytoken
Detect unauthorized access attempts
Track lateral movement within your network
Analyze credential cracking techniques
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: A honeytoken is fake data—often a credential, API key, database value, or identifier—that has no legitimate use. Any use of it is suspicious.
course.why: Honeytokens are lightweight and can reveal credential theft or lateral movement quickly.
course.example: A fake cloud access key is placed in a monitored repository. An alert fires if anyone attempts to authenticate with it.
course.exam: The key clue is decoy data or credentials rather than a complete decoy host.

breakdown.explanation: This concerns who or what can reach a resource and what actions are permitted once access is granted.
